title: These Seals Are Doing Oceanography (And They Don't Even Know It)
summary: Imagine strapping a tiny sensor to a seal's forehead and letting it dive into the freezing Southern Ocean. That's not a sci-fi movie — it's real science. Oceanographer Lily Dove studies how climate change affects the Southern Ocean, the vast ocean circling Antarctica. But instead of diving herself, she used data from the Marine Mammals Exploring the Oceans Pole to Pole program. This international team attaches sensors to southern elephant and Weddell seals. The seals dive more than 100 meters (330 feet) deep to find food, collecting data on temperature, salinity, and pressure along the way. "They're oceanographers," Dove says. "They are regularly making dives in areas that we don't often get to sample." The animals don't seem bothered by the sensors. In certain parts of the Southern Ocean, heat from the atmosphere sinks into the deep ocean and gets trapped there for hundreds of years, slowly warming the planet. Dove used the seals' data to track this process. Now at the Georgia Institute of Technology, she works with autonomous robots instead. Some, called floats, drift with currents. Others, called gliders, can be piloted remotely. "I can sit here in Georgia and tell my glider in a whole different hemisphere where I want it to go," she says. But gliders are more predictable than seals. "Seals very much tell me where they want to go," she jokes. Dove also shared her advice for young scientists: say yes to opportunities, learn broadly, and don't be afraid to speak up. She faced discrimination as a woman in polar science, but she learned to advocate for herself. Her story shows that curiosity — and a little help from some furry friends — can lead to big discoveries.
why_it_matters: The deep Southern Ocean is one of the planet's main brakes on warming, and much of it is too icy and remote for ships to survey properly — so animal-borne sensors and robot fleets quietly shape what climate models can predict. The story also shows that who gets to do polar science matters: Dove's experience of discrimination points to a field that still has to change to use all the talent available.

background_read: The Southern Ocean is the water that encircles Antarctica; it links the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans and is now commonly listed as Earth's fifth ocean. The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the strongest current on the planet, flows through it, and the region soaks up a large share of the extra heat trapped in the atmosphere by greenhouse gases.

Southern elephant seals are the largest of all seals, with adult males weighing several tons, while Weddell seals are known for living farther south than any other mammal and for diving beneath sea ice. Both species dive deep and repeatedly, which is why they make useful data collectors in places ships and people rarely reach.

The Marine Mammals Exploring the Oceans Pole to Pole program is an international effort in which researchers share data gathered by sensors temporarily attached to seals, turning thousands of animal dives into a public ocean dataset. Tagged seals have been used this way since the 1990s, and the sensors are designed to fall off when the animal molts.

Lily Dove now works at the Georgia Institute of Technology — a university in Atlanta, in the U.S. state of Georgia, not the country of Georgia — where she uses autonomous robots. Floats drift passively with currents while gliders can be steered from another hemisphere, but neither chooses its own route the way a seal does.

Women were once largely excluded from Antarctic research stations, and although that has changed, studies of polar science have repeatedly found harassment and discrimination remain problems. Dove's account of learning to advocate for herself fits a broader push to make fieldwork safer and more inclusive.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — cheap, deep and wide coverage
perspectives.description: Seals go where research vessels cannot: under ice, in winter, far from any port. For the cost of a small tag, scientists get thousands of deep profiles of temperature and salinity, and the data are shared internationally through programs like MEOP. Dove's use of the data to trace how heat sinks into the deep ocean shows how much science can come from an existing, freely available dataset.

Attaching instruments to wild animals raises real welfare questions, even if the animals appear undisturbed and the tags are designed to fall off. There is also a sampling problem: seals dive where they hunt, not where scientists would choose, so the data are unevenly spread and could bias conclusions about the wider ocean. Robot fleets, by contrast, can be sent to targets chosen in advance.

Using animals as oceanographers is not brand new; researchers have deployed tags on seals and other marine mammals for decades, gradually building an archive that satellites and floats alone could not provide. The story reflects a broader shift in ocean science from ship-based expeditions toward a mix of autonomous floats, gliders and animals, all feeding shared databases. It also illustrates how climate questions drive methods: the need to measure the deep Southern Ocean is what made seals so valuable.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — robots, data and who gets to work
perspectives.description: The next decade will likely combine larger fleets of autonomous gliders and floats with continued animal tagging, and better models to merge the two data streams. Dove's advice — say yes, learn broadly, speak up — points at another needed change: polar science is still working to become welcoming to women and other underrepresented groups. How quickly that changes will shape both the questions asked and who is credited with answering them.
